analysis.title: Our latest views on the major central banks
key_insights: ING expects the Fed to hike once more at the December FOMC meeting, then pause for a prolonged period well into 2027. The Fed hiked in September and signalled at least one more increase.

Markets priced in at least three additional 25bp Fed moves after the September hike. Pricing has become more cautious because officials skipped the October FOMC meeting despite higher-than-expected inflation prints.

Fed officials are near-uniform in saying there is no immediate pressure to hike. ING cites evidence that interest-rate-sensitive parts of the economy are cooling and wage pressures look increasingly benign.
ING argues that further Fed hikes will not ease Middle East tensions and will do little to cool the strong pipeline of tech investment.

Another ECB rate hike in December looks like a done deal to ING. The 2027 outlook is less certain and depends on the intensity and duration of the Middle East war and on how far higher energy prices feed into broader inflation.

ING's ECB base case is that energy prices fall in 2027 and weak final demand limits companies' pricing power, so the inflation wave stays mainly an energy price shock. The ECB could hold in 2027 and might consider a rate cut toward the end of the year.
ING expects one more BoE hike in February, after the BoE's first hike since 2023 in early November. It does not rule out a December hike if the energy crisis worsens. UK inflation is headed above 4%.

ING sees little evidence of second-round effects in the UK: food inflation is benign, its gauge of energy-intensive inflation is down this year, and the cool jobs market limits wage pressure. If minimal signs persist through the April CPI report (released in May), the BoE could turn dovish by summer and cut before the end of 2027.

The BoJ reached its 2% inflation target in October, a target set in 2013. The policy rate is 1.25% and neutral is commonly seen at 1.75-2.00%. ING expects 25bp hikes at the December and March meetings.

Market pricing for the BoJ is more aggressive than ING's, with a 2.00% policy rate expected next summer. ING thinks 1.75% may be enough because government support measures will weigh on headline inflation from next April, and government pressure against excessive tightening will rise.

ING expects the PBoC to stay in easing mode despite global tightening. It cites inflation likely under 1% by year-end against a 2% target, domestic activity data at the weakest since the pandemic, and a soft labour market with high youth unemployment.
The PBoC has preferred targeted easing to policy rate cuts. ING sees scope for both in 2027, especially if external demand weakens, and forecasts a 10bp rate cut in mid-2027.

macro_indicators.reading: One more 25bp hike in December 2026, then a prolonged pause into 2027
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING expects the Fed to end hikes in December, while markets had priced at least three more 25bp moves after September.

macro_indicators.reading: Rate hike in December 2026, possible cut toward end of 2027
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING sees the December hike as a done deal and a hold through most of 2027 if energy prices fall.

macro_indicators.reading: One more hike in February 2027, possible hike in December 2026, cut before end of 2027
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING expects tightening to continue near term and an easing turn later in 2027 if second-round effects stay minimal.
Energy-driven inflation is the reason the BoE is considering further hikes.

macro_indicators.reading: 1.25% current, 25bp hikes in December and March, to 1.75%
macro_indicators.interpretation: ING's terminal rate is below the 2.00% policy rate the market expects by next summer.
Current policy rate, below the 1.75-2.00% range commonly seen as neutral.
BoJ hit its 2% target for the first time since it was set in 2013, which keeps normalisation going.
Inflation well below the 2% target supports further PBoC easing.
ING expects a small cut after a preference for targeted easing over rate cuts.

risk_factors: Intensity and duration of the Middle East war and the path of energy prices.
Pass-through of higher energy prices into broader inflation, which the ECB expects in 2027.
UK energy crisis worsening, which could bring a BoE hike in December.
Second-round effects in UK inflation, to be tested by the April CPI report released in May.
Government pressure to avoid excessive tightening in Japan.
vol_and_positioning: Markets priced at least three additional 25bp Fed hikes after the September hike, and pricing has become more cautious since the October FOMC meeting was skipped.
BoJ market pricing is for a 2.00% policy rate next summer, above ING's 1.75% forecast.
geopolitical: War in the Middle East and the resulting energy crisis are the main driver of ECB and BoE inflation outlooks.
ING says further Fed hikes will do nothing to ease tensions in the Middle East.

tension_points.bull_case: Strong growth, low unemployment and above-target inflation prompted a September hike and a signal of at least one more, and markets priced at least three additional 25bp moves.
tension_points.bear_case: Rate-sensitive parts of the economy are cooling, wage pressure is benign, and officials skipped the October FOMC meeting, so ING sees only one more hike in December.

tension_points.bull_case: Inflation is headed above 4% and the Bank is worried the energy crisis is deep and long enough to justify more hikes, possibly in December.
tension_points.bear_case: Food inflation is benign, energy-intensive inflation is down this year, and the cool jobs market limits wage pressure, which could allow a dovish turn by summer.
tension_points.what_invalidates: If the April CPI report released in May still shows minimal signs of second-round effects, ING expects the BoE to turn more dovish by summer.

theme_stances.evidence: the ECB can keep its powder dry in 2027
